terms.grammar: pronoun, second person plural: dative and ablative vōbīs
evidence: Liv. 1.56.10: quī vestrum prīmus … ōsculum mātrī tulerit
terms.comment: Said only to more than one person. Left out like tū unless stressed. Of the two genitives, vestrum means “of you” as a part of the group (quis vestrum, which of you; ūnusquisque vestrum), vestrī is the object of a feeling or a thought (memor vestrī, mindful of you). “With you” is vōbīscum.

phrases.english: My dear Geta, I love you all.
What, you haven’t had dinner yet?

phrases.latin: vōs hīc hodiē cēnātōte ambō. — Fīat. — Plausum date.
phrases.english: You two will dine here tonight, both of you. — So be it. — Give us your applause.

phrases.latin: imperium summum Rōmae habēbit quī vestrum prīmus, ō juvenēs, ōsculum mātrī tulerit
phrases.english: Whichever of you, young men, is the first to kiss his mother shall hold the highest power at Rome.

phrases.latin: vōs, meae cārissimae animae, quam saepissimē ad mē scrībite et vōs quid agātis et quid istīc agātur
phrases.english: You, my dearest souls, write to me as often as you can, both how you are and what is going on there.

phrases.latin: Bene ambulētis, et sit Deus in itinere vestrō, et angelus ejus comitētur vōbīscum.
phrases.english: Have a good journey; God be on your way, and his angel go with you.
